contradictions.question: Did Mary Magdalene recognize Jesus when he first appeared to her?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:9 has Mary and the other Mary meet the risen Jesus, grab his feet, and worship him — no confusion, instant recognition. John 20:14 has Mary Magdalene look right at him and not realize who he is, mistaking him for the gardener. Luke 24:23 throws a third curve: in Luke's version Mary doesn't see Jesus at the tomb at all, only a vision of angels. Three Gospels, three incompatible accounts of the same moment.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction sits right at the foundational event of Christianity, and the harmonizers know it, which is why the apologist playbook here is so creative. Gleason Archer (Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, Zondervan 1982, pp. 347-349) and Norman Geisler argue these are sequential encounters — first Jesus blocks Mary from recognizing him in John, then later in Matthew she sees him clearly with the other Mary. The problem is that this requires reading the texts as a single composite narrative the evangelists themselves never wrote. Matthew has the women, plural, meet Jesus on the way back from the tomb after seeing the angel. John has Mary alone, returning a second time after fetching Peter and the Beloved Disciple. These are not two scenes you can stack on top of each other without rewriting both. And Luke is even worse for the harmonizer — in Luke 24:22-24 the women report seeing angels who said Jesus was alive, not Jesus himself, and the men later go check the tomb and find it empty without anyone meeting the risen Christ there. That is of course Luke's editorial choice, but it directly contradicts both Matthew and John on whether Jesus appeared at the tomb at all. The critical consensus, from Raymond Brown forward, is that each evangelist is shaping the resurrection appearances to serve his own theological program — Matthew's high Christology demands immediate worship, John's stresses recognition through hearing the Shepherd's voice, Luke's emphasizes the witness of angels and the disciples' slowness to believe. The differences are not chronological gaps the reader is supposed to fill in; they are the data.

contradictions.question: Where did Jesus tell his disciples to go after his resurrection?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:10 and Mark 16:7 have Jesus (or his angelic messenger) tell the disciples to head north to Galilee — that's where they'll see him. Luke 24:49 and Acts 1:4 have the risen Jesus give the opposite instruction: stay in Jerusalem and wait for the Spirit. Same person, same window of time, two directly incompatible commands.
contradictions.commentary: This one is geographically clean and that is why it is so damaging. Galilee is roughly 70 miles north of Jerusalem. You cannot simultaneously command someone to leave a city and remain in it. Craig Blomberg (The Historical Reliability of the Gospels, IVP Academic 2007, pp. 145-149) and the standard harmonization route runs like this: the disciples first went to Galilee for the appearances Matthew describes, then returned to Jerusalem in time for the Luke 24:49 commission and Pentecost. The problem is that Luke's text does not allow it. Luke 24 collapses the entire post-resurrection sequence — appearance to the Emmaus disciples, return to Jerusalem, appearance to the eleven, ascension — into what reads as a single day, with the Galilee command in Mark and Matthew nowhere on Luke's map. And Acts 1:4 explicitly says Jesus commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem. Not 'come back after a side trip.' Don't depart. Source-critically, the consensus diagnosis is that Luke-Acts and Matthew-Mark preserve two independent and incompatible resurrection traditions — one centered on Galilean appearances (the earlier and probably more historical strand, since Galilee is where the movement started) and one centered on Jerusalem appearances (which serves Luke's theological project of making Jerusalem the launching point for the Gentile mission). Rudolf Bultmann, Hans Conzelmann, and more recently Dale Allison have all read it that way. The harmonization requires inserting a Galilee trip into Luke's narrative that Luke himself shows no awareness of, and overriding Acts 1:4's explicit prohibition. That is post-hoc rationalization, not exegesis.

contradictions.question: To whom did Jesus make his first post-resurrection appearance?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:9 says the first appearance was to the two Marys together. Mark 16:9 and John 20:14-17 say it was Mary Magdalene alone. Luke 24:13-31 has the first identified appearance happen to Cleopas and an unnamed companion on the road to Emmaus. Paul, writing the earliest of these texts, names Cephas (Peter) as the first witness in 1 Corinthians 15:5 and never mentions any of the women at all.
contradictions.commentary: Four sources, four different answers to the most basic possible question about the central miracle of Christianity. The harmonizers usually attack this one by stacking the appearances chronologically — Mary Magdalene first, then the two Marys together, then Peter, then Emmaus — and waving away Paul's silence on Mary Magdalene as a culturally embarrassing omission. Gary Habermas (The Risen Jesus and Future Hope, Rowman & Littlefield 2003) defends this stacking approach extensively. The first problem is internal: Mark 16:9 explicitly says Jesus 'appeared first to Mary Magdalene,' which directly contradicts both Matthew's two-Mary version and Paul's Cephas-first creed. The second problem is that the Mark 16:9-20 'longer ending' is not original to Mark — it is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus), as Bruce Metzger documents in detail, which means apologists are leaning on a second-century addition to harmonize the first-century texts. The third and biggest problem is Paul. 1 Corinthians 15:3-7 is, by near-universal scholarly consensus, the earliest written tradition we have about the resurrection, dating to within a few years of the crucifixion. Paul says he 'received' this creed and then 'delivered' it — formal language for transmitting an authoritative tradition. And the creed names Cephas first. No women at all. The standard apologetic reply, that women's testimony was inadmissible in court so Paul left them out, fails for two reasons: women's testimony was admissible in many first-century Jewish legal contexts, and Paul is reciting a creed for the church, not testifying at a Roman trial. The simpler reading — the parsimonious one — is that the women-at-the-tomb tradition and the Cephas-first tradition developed independently in different Christian communities and the Gospel writers each had to choose which one to feature. That is of course a critical-scholarly judgment, but the textual evidence runs heavily that direction.

contradictions.question: How many disciples did Jesus appear to in his first post resurrection appearance?
contradictions.summary: John 20:24 says Thomas was absent when Jesus first appeared to the group, so with Judas already dead (Matthew 27:5) the count is ten. Matthew 28:16-17, Mark 16:14, and Luke 24:33-37 all say 'the eleven' were present. Paul, writing earliest, says Jesus appeared to 'the twelve' (1 Corinthians 15:5), which is impossible given that Judas is gone and Matthias has not yet been chosen.
contradictions.commentary: Three different numbers, and the worst one is Paul's. The standard harmonization, defended by Craig Blomberg and Norman Geisler, treats 'the twelve' in 1 Corinthians 15:5 as a fixed titular designation for the apostolic college regardless of actual membership count — like calling the U.S. Senate 'the hundred' even when there's a vacant seat. Anthony Thiselton's NIGTC commentary on 1 Corinthians (Eerdmans 2000, pp. 1204-1205) makes the strongest version of this case, noting that some manuscripts read 'the eleven' rather than 'the twelve,' which would be a scribal harmonization with the Gospels. That manuscript variant is real, but the critical text reads 'the twelve' precisely because 'the eleven' is the easier reading and scribes don't tend to make texts harder. The titular-designation argument has some merit but it does not resolve the underlying problem: Paul shows no awareness of any of the Gospel resurrection scenes. He doesn't know about Thomas being absent, doesn't mention any women, doesn't situate the appearances geographically. He gives a creedal list — Cephas, the twelve, five hundred at once, James, all the apostles, then me — that reads like an independent tradition. The Gospel numbers (ten in John, eleven in the Synoptics) reflect a later narrative tradition that had developed Judas's death and Thomas's absence into the story. The simpler reading is that Paul's creed predates these narrative details and Paul didn't know them. The harmonizer's appeal to 'the twelve' as a title is doing real work — but it cannot reconcile Paul with John's specific claim that Thomas was missing. Take your pick: either Paul didn't know the Thomas tradition (parsimonious, fits the chronology) or 'the twelve' is shorthand for 'whoever happened to be in the room' (ad hoc).

contradictions.question: Where did Jesus first appear to the eleven disciples after the resurrection?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:16 says the eleven met Jesus on a mountain in Galilee — a multi-day journey from the tomb. Mark 16:14, Luke 24:33-37, and John 20:19 all locate the first group appearance to the eleven in a room in Jerusalem, on the day of the resurrection itself. Same scene, two different cities seventy miles apart.
contradictions.commentary: This is the geographic problem from contradiction 482, only sharper. Matthew's resurrection narrative has exactly one appearance to the disciples and it happens on a Galilean mountain. Luke and John's narratives have the first appearance to the group happen in Jerusalem the same Sunday. The standard apologist move, articulated by Wenham (Easter Enigma, Paternoster 1984) and Blomberg, is to harmonize by claiming Matthew skipped the Jerusalem appearance entirely and jumped to a later Galilean one. The problem is that Matthew's text gives no indication of such a jump. Matthew 28:16 reads as the disciples' immediate response to the resurrection command — they 'went into Galilee' to the appointed mountain, and that is where Jesus 'appointed them.' There is no Jerusalem detour, no Pentecost setup, no doubting Thomas. Matthew ends with this single mountaintop scene and the Great Commission. Meanwhile John explicitly says the first appearance to the gathered disciples was 'the same day at evening' in a locked room in Jerusalem (John 20:19). Both texts cannot be describing the first encounter unless one of them is wrong. The critical consensus from Bultmann through Brown is that the Galilean tradition (Matthew, hinted at in Mark 16:7) and the Jerusalem tradition (Luke and John) developed independently in different early communities, and the canonical Gospels preserve them side by side without successfully integrating them. Trying to stitch them into a single timeline is the apologist playbook, page one — but the seams show.

contradictions.question: What did Jesus do after his baptism?
contradictions.summary: Mark 1:12-13 says the Spirit immediately drove Jesus into the wilderness for forty days of temptation right after his baptism. John 1:35-2:1 has Jesus on day two calling disciples and on day three attending a wedding at Cana — no wilderness, no forty-day fast, no satanic temptation. Same Jesus, same post-baptism window, two incompatible itineraries.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is sharp because Mark uses the Greek word euthus — 'immediately' — to mark the temporal sequence. Mark 1:12 literally says 'and immediately the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness.' No gap allowed. John's narrative, by contrast, gives a day-by-day chronology that places Jesus among John the Baptist's followers the day after the baptism, then in Galilee gathering disciples, then at a wedding in Cana on day three. Forty days of solitary fasting cannot fit anywhere in John's chronology. The standard harmonization, found in D. A. Carson's PNTC commentary on John (Eerdmans 1991, pp. 146-149) and earlier in Leon Morris, is to insert the forty-day temptation before John 1:35 — claiming John picks up the narrative after the wilderness episode is already over. This requires the baptism itself to have happened before John 1:19, somewhere off-page, and Jesus to have spent forty days in the wilderness between that off-page baptism and the day John 1 actually starts recounting. The text gives no hint of any of this. John 1:32-34 has the Baptist describing the descent of the Spirit at Jesus' baptism as if it just happened, then on 'the next day' (1:35) Jesus walks past with disciples in tow. There is no forty-day gap to be found unless you invent one. The simpler reading is that John's Gospel preserves a different and independent tradition about Jesus' early ministry that knows nothing of the wilderness temptation. That is the consensus reading from Raymond Brown through Bart Ehrman. Mark's wilderness account itself has clear theological function — Jesus as the new Israel re-tested for forty (years/days) in the desert — and the Synoptic versions in Matthew and Luke elaborate it heavily. John dropped the scene because it didn't serve his theological program of the cosmic Logos who needs no testing. Two early traditions, two Christologies, one impossible composite.

contradictions.question: Are those who believe Jesus is the Christ of God?
contradictions.summary: First John lays down the test plainly: anyone who confesses that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, is born of God and indwelt by God (1 John 4:2, 4:15, 5:1). But the Synoptic Gospels show unclean spirits and demons doing exactly that — Mark 1:23-24, Mark 3:11, Mark 5:7, Luke 4:34, Luke 4:41 all have demons publicly confessing Jesus as the Holy One of God, the Son of God, the Christ. James 2:19 makes it explicit: 'the devils also believe, and tremble.' By the Johannine criterion, the demons would qualify as born of God.
contradictions.commentary: The question text is awkwardly phrased — it should probably read 'Are those who believe Jesus is the Christ of God?' meaning 'do they belong to God?' — but the underlying contradiction is real and the references support it. 1 John 4:2 gives a sharp doctrinal litmus: confession of the incarnation marks the Spirit of God. 1 John 4:15 and 5:1 reinforce that anyone confessing this is indwelt and born of God. The author of 1 John clearly intends this as a criterion of authentic faith against the Docetists or proto-Gnostic opponents who denied a fleshly Christ. The problem is that the Synoptic demons pass the test. They identify Jesus as 'the Holy One of God' (Mark 1:24), 'the Son of God' (Mark 3:11), 'Jesus, thou Son of the most high God' (Mark 5:7), and 'Christ the Son of God' (Luke 4:41). These are not vague acknowledgments — they are precisely the confessional content 1 John makes salvific. The standard apologetic move, from Calvin onward, is to distinguish intellectual assent (demons) from saving faith (believers). James 2:19 is then read as supporting this distinction. The problem is that 1 John 4:2 and 4:15 do not condition the test on the heart-attitude of the confessor. The text says 'every spirit that confesses' and 'whosoever shall confess' — universal language, no qualifier. The author of 1 John appears unaware that demons make the same confession in the Synoptic tradition, which is unsurprising if 1 John and the Synoptics are drawing on different theological streams. The simpler reading is that the Johannine epistle's confessional test was forged against a specific second-generation opponent (Docetism) without the author thinking through whether demonic confessions would satisfy the criterion. Once you hold the texts side by side, they don't agree.

contradictions.question: Where was the home of Peter and Andrew?
contradictions.summary: Mark 1:21, 29 puts the house of Simon and Andrew in Capernaum, where Jesus teaches in the synagogue and then walks straight to their home. John 1:44 says Bethsaida was 'the city of Andrew and Peter.' Two different towns, several miles apart on opposite sides of the Jordan's outlet into the Sea of Galilee.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologetic harmonization, defended by D. A. Carson and earlier by Leon Morris, distinguishes between hometown of origin (Bethsaida, where the brothers were raised) and place of residence at the time of Jesus' ministry (Capernaum, where Peter's house with his mother-in-law was located). This is a plausible reading of John 1:44 if you press the Greek polis ('city') to mean 'birthplace' rather than 'current residence,' and most modern Bible difficulty manuals run with it. The strongest version of this argument is reasonable on the face of it — people relocate, and a fisherman moving a few miles along the lake shore would be unremarkable. The harmonization has real exegetical weight. But there is a second-order problem the apologists generally don't address: the geography in the Synoptics versus John is in tension on other points too. Mark consistently treats Bethsaida as a separate destination from Capernaum (Mark 6:45, 8:22), suggesting the two towns are distinct in his narrative world without overlapping resident populations. John 12:21 also identifies Philip 'of Bethsaida' alongside Andrew, treating them as a unit from that town. The simpler hypothesis is that John's Gospel is drawing on a tradition that places the early disciples in Bethsaida (consistent with its placement of John the Baptist's activity nearby in 'Bethany beyond the Jordan'), while Mark's tradition has Capernaum as the operational base. The contradiction is real but mild — it is one of the easier-to-harmonize entries in the gospel cycle, and a critical scholar should be honest that the relocation hypothesis is defensible even if it leaves source-critical questions on the table.

contradictions.question: Where did the devils ask not to go?
contradictions.summary: Mark 5:9-10 has Legion beg Jesus not to send the demons 'out of the country.' Luke 8:30-31, telling the same story, has them beg not to be sent 'into the deep' (abyssos — the abyss). The geographic plea in Mark and the cosmological plea in Luke are not the same request.
contradictions.commentary: This is a small but telling editorial difference. Mark's version reads as a local-spatial plea — don't expel us from this region. Luke's abyssos is loaded theological vocabulary: in the Septuagint and apocalyptic literature, the abyss is the cosmic prison for rebellious spirits (compare Revelation 9:1-2, 11; 20:1-3; 1 Enoch 18-21). Luke is shifting Mark's mundane geographic request into a cosmological one about the eschatological imprisonment of demons. The standard apologetic move, present in I. Howard Marshall's NIGTC commentary on Luke (Eerdmans 1978, pp. 337-339), treats these as complementary — the demons asked both, and each evangelist preserved one strand. That is a possible reading, but it is also the harmonizer's reflex: when two parallel texts disagree, assume both happened. The simpler explanation, which is the consensus in the Synoptic Problem literature, is that Luke is editing Mark to fit a more developed demonology. Joseph Fitzmyer's Anchor Bible commentary on Luke notes that abyssos is a Lukan addition reflecting his theological framework. The contradiction is mild on its own — both versions agree the demons didn't want to be cast out into something — but it is part of a larger pattern of Luke systematically theologizing Mark's source material. That is not an attack on inerrancy in itself, but it does undermine the claim that the Synoptic accounts are independent eyewitness reports. They are not. Luke is reworking Mark, and this verse is one of the cleaner pieces of evidence for that.

contradictions.question: Where did Jesus cure the blind man?
contradictions.summary: PRELIM FLAG: The cited passages describe two distinct healing miracles, not one event with conflicting locations. Mark 8:22-25 narrates the two-stage healing of the Bethsaida blind man (Jesus spits on his eyes, the man sees 'men as trees walking,' then is healed clearly with a second touch). John 9, with the introductory verses at John 8:59, narrates the healing of a man born blind, performed outside the temple in Jerusalem using clay made from spittle and a wash in the pool of Siloam. The two stories share only the genre of 'blind man healed by Jesus.' The narrative details, the location, the method, and even the patient's history all differ. The Gospels narrate multiple distinct blindness healings (the two blind men at Jericho in Matthew 20:30, blind Bartimaeus in Mark 10:46, the unnamed blind man at Bethsaida in Mark 8, the man born blind in John 9), and the contradiction-question as framed treats these as if they were the same event with conflicting locations. They are not.
contradictions.commentary: PRELIM FLAG: This entry is incoherent as stated. The 'contradiction' depends on conflating two different miracle narratives into one. A genuine 'location-of-the-blind-man' contradiction would require parallel accounts of the same healing event giving incompatible locations — for example, comparing Matthew 20:29-34 (Jesus heals two blind men as he is leaving Jericho) with Mark 10:46-52 (Jesus heals one blind man, named Bartimaeus, as he is leaving Jericho) with Luke 18:35-43 (Jesus heals one blind man as he is approaching Jericho). That trio is a real contradiction about a single healing episode. Mark 8 versus John 9 is not. There is no overlap in narrative detail between Mark's Bethsaida miracle and John's man-born-blind miracle. Recommend either rewriting the question to address the Jericho contradiction or marking this entry for deletion. The current framing also lets apologists win the argument by pointing out the obvious fact that Jesus healed many blind people in many places, which the Gospels themselves explicitly acknowledge (Matthew 15:30-31; Luke 7:21).

contradictions.question: Who can cast out devils in the name of Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Mark 16:17 says exorcism in Jesus' name is a sign that follows 'them that believe' — a believers-only operation. Matthew 7:21-23, Mark 9:38, and Luke 9:49 all describe people casting out demons in Jesus' name who are explicitly not part of his followers — including some whom Jesus rejects at the final judgment despite their successful exorcisms ('I never knew you').
contradictions.commentary: The clearest case is Matthew 7:21-23. Jesus describes people who will say, on the last day, 'have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils?' and his answer is not 'no you didn't' — it's 'depart from me, ye that work iniquity.' The exorcisms happened. Jesus just doesn't accept the exorcists. That is a direct denial of the Mark 16:17 claim that successful exorcism marks genuine belief. Mark 9:38 and Luke 9:49 reinforce the point: an unaffiliated exorcist is using Jesus' name effectively, and Jesus' response is 'forbid him not.' The apologist harmonization here, found in William Lane's NICNT commentary on Mark (Eerdmans 1974, pp. 601-611) and in Craig Blomberg, distinguishes between 'belief' as inner saving faith versus mere invocation of a powerful name. On this reading, Mark 16:17 promises the sign to true believers while Matthew 7 and Mark 9 describe outsiders successfully wielding the name without saving faith. That distinction has theological coherence, but it runs into two problems. First, Mark 16:17 is part of the longer ending of Mark, which is missing from the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and is universally recognized as a second-century addition. So the contradiction is partly a contradiction between a late textual addition and the earlier canonical material. Second, the early Christian community clearly did believe that the name of Jesus was a power-laden formula that worked regardless of the wielder's inner state — see the sons of Sceva episode in Acts 19:13-16, where outsiders try the formula and it backfires. The picture in the Synoptics is that the name has power that can be wielded by outsiders, which contradicts the Markan-ending's tighter linkage of exorcism to belief. The longer ending is harmonizing for a later church that wanted to draw the lines more tightly.

contradictions.question: When was the Holy Ghost given?
contradictions.summary: John 7:39 says outright that 'the Holy Ghost was not yet given; because that Jesus was not yet glorified.' John 20:22 has Jesus breathe the Spirit onto the disciples post-resurrection. Acts 2:1-4 has the Spirit arrive at Pentecost in tongues of fire. But Mark 12:36 has David speaking by the Holy Ghost in the Psalms, Luke 1:15 has John the Baptist filled with the Spirit from the womb, Luke 1:41 has Elizabeth filled with the Spirit, Luke 1:67 has Zacharias filled with the Spirit, and Luke 2:25 has the Holy Ghost upon Simeon — all centuries or decades before Jesus is glorified.
contradictions.commentary: John 7:39 is the smoking gun because it makes a categorical theological claim: the Spirit has not yet been given. That is incompatible with Luke's infancy narratives, where the Spirit is given liberally to Elizabeth, Zacharias, John, and Simeon before Jesus has even started ministry, let alone been glorified. The standard apologetic move, articulated by D. A. Carson in his John commentary (PNTC, Eerdmans 1991, pp. 328-329) and earlier by Bishop Westcott, distinguishes between the Spirit's individual empowerings (pre-Pentecost) and the corporate indwelling of the Spirit (post-Pentecost). On this reading, the Old Testament and Lukan figures received the Spirit episodically for specific tasks, while the Pentecost gift is the new-covenant permanent indwelling. That distinction has real theological coherence in systematic theology. The problem is John 7:39 will not bend to it. The Greek is unambiguous: oupō gar ēn pneuma — 'for there was not yet Spirit.' Some manuscripts add 'given' or 'holy' but the underlying claim is the same: the Spirit is not yet operative. John does not say 'the Spirit was not yet given in its new-covenant corporate form.' He says it was not yet. That is a categorical denial that any of the Lukan or Old Testament figures could have been Spirit-filled in any sense. The simpler reading is that John is working with a high-Christology framework where the Spirit is tied specifically to the post-glorification Christ, and he is in tension with the Synoptic and Old Testament traditions that operate with a broader pneumatology. The harmonization saves the inerrancy claim, but only by reading distinctions into John 7:39 that the text does not make. The narrative contradiction is also live: John 20:22 has the Spirit given on resurrection Sunday by Jesus' breath; Acts 2 has it given fifty days later in tongues of fire. Both are 'the giving of the Spirit' to the same group. Pick one.

contradictions.question: When (on what day) was Jesus crucified?
contradictions.summary: John 18:28 has the chief priests refusing to enter Pilate's praetorium 'lest they should be defiled; but that they might eat the passover' — meaning the Passover meal has not yet happened. John 19:14 confirms it: the crucifixion occurs on 'the preparation of the passover.' But Mark 14:12 has Jesus' last supper as the Passover meal itself ('the first day of unleavened bread, when they killed the passover'), and Mark 15:25 has the crucifixion at the third hour the following morning — meaning Jesus was crucified the day after the Passover meal. John puts the crucifixion before Passover; the Synoptics put it after.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the oldest known and most-discussed contradictions in the New Testament, and the scholarly consensus is that it is real and unresolvable by harmonization. The Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) all clearly portray the Last Supper as a Passover meal, eaten on the evening of Nisan 14 (which by Jewish reckoning begins the day of Nisan 15), with the crucifixion happening the following morning on Nisan 15. John's Gospel, with equal clarity, has Jesus crucified at the time the Passover lambs are being slaughtered in the temple on Nisan 14 — making the Last Supper a pre-Passover meal, not the Passover itself. The theological motivation in John is transparent: Jesus is the Lamb of God (John 1:29, 36), and John times the crucifixion to make Jesus die at the exact hour the Passover lambs are killed. Joachim Jeremias (The Eucharistic Words of Jesus, SCM 1966) defended the Synoptic chronology as historical and treated John's as theological reshaping. Most modern critical scholars (Brown, Meier, Sanders) treat the contradiction as genuine and lean toward John's chronology being closer to historical — partly because a Sanhedrin trial on the night of Passover is implausible under Jewish law (m. Sanhedrin 4:1), partly because the Synoptic Passover-meal framing serves their own theological purposes (eucharistic institution). The standard harmonization attempts include the Qumran-calendar theory (Annie Jaubert, La Date de la Cène, Gabalda 1957) — that Jesus followed a sectarian solar calendar and held his Passover earlier than the temple's — and the lexical claim that 'eat the Passover' in John 18:28 could mean the chagigah sacrifice rather than the Passover lamb proper. The Jaubert theory has never gained majority support; the lexical move strains John's plain meaning. The cleaner reading: the two traditions diverge for theological reasons and the Gospels are not reconcilable on this point.

contradictions.question: Did the cock crow before or after Peter's denial?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 26:74, Luke 22:60, and John 18:27 all have the cock crow after Peter's third denial. Mark 14:67-72 has the cock crow after the first denial and then a second time after the third — and Jesus' prediction in Mark 14:30 specifies 'before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice.' Three Gospels have one cock-crow at the end of the sequence; Mark has two, with the first happening after denial number one.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction sits between Mark and the rest of the synoptic tradition. Mark 14:30 has Jesus predict 'before the cock crow twice' — a two-crow sequence. Matthew, Luke, and John all flatten this to a single crow at the end. The Markan account is internally consistent: the cock crows after denial one (Mark 14:68 in the Majority Text and TR, though this verse is missing from some early manuscripts including Sinaiticus), and again after denial three (Mark 14:72), matching the 'crow twice' prediction in Mark 14:30. The other Gospels appear to have edited Mark to simplify the prediction and the fulfillment. The standard apologetic move, defended by Gleason Archer (Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, Zondervan 1982, pp. 343-345) and earlier by John Wenham, is to argue Mark preserves the more detailed account and the others abbreviate. That is technically a non-contradiction defense: if Mark is more detailed and the others omit the first crow without denying it, no formal contradiction obtains. The weakness of this defense is that Jesus' prediction itself differs across the Gospels — Matthew 26:34 and Luke 22:34 have him predict a single crow ('before the cock crow') while Mark 14:30 has him predict two ('before the cock crow twice'). Jesus cannot have predicted both. One evangelist is preserving the original logion and the others have changed it, or vice versa. The textual situation is also messy — Mark 14:68's reference to the first crow is missing from some manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus), which Bruce Metzger argues is the original Markan text and the addition is a later scribal harmonization. If Metzger is right, even Mark originally had only one crow, and the doubled crow in the textus receptus is itself a harmonizing intrusion. Either way, the predictions don't match across the Gospels. That is the underlying contradiction the harmonizers cannot escape.

contradictions.question: When did the Temple veil rip?
contradictions.summary: Luke 23:45-46 puts the tearing of the temple veil before Jesus dies: the sun darkens, the veil rips, and then Jesus commends his spirit and gives up the ghost. Matthew 27:50-51 and Mark 15:37-38 reverse the sequence: Jesus cries out and dies first, and then the veil tears.
contradictions.commentary: Read the texts side by side and the sequence is clean. Luke's grammar puts the veil-tearing in the middle of the darkening of the sun, before Jesus' final cry and death. Matthew and Mark both have Jesus die first and then describe the veil tearing as the immediate response to his death. The standard apologetic harmonization, defended in Craig Blomberg's The Historical Reliability of the Gospels (IVP Academic 2007, pp. 155-156), is to treat the ordering as loose — ancient writers, the argument runs, were not concerned with strict chronological sequence and could mention events thematically rather than temporally. There is some truth to this in general; ancient narrative does sometimes operate non-linearly. But Luke has done the thing intentionally. He has rearranged the Markan order to put the veil-tearing as part of the cosmic darkness that accompanies the crucifixion, before the death, while Mark and Matthew place it as the divine response to the death itself. This is not random; it is theological editing. Joseph Fitzmyer's Anchor Bible commentary on Luke argues Luke is reshaping the scene to group the cosmic signs (sun-darkening, veil-tearing) into a single ominous prelude, with Jesus' death and final words as the climax. Mark's order, where the veil tears as God's reaction to the death, fits Mark's theology of the cross as the moment of revelation. Luke's order serves Luke's theology of Jesus' death as a serene, controlled commendation of spirit to the Father. Both evangelists are arranging the elements for effect, and the arrangements are incompatible. The minor-order harmonization is reasonable on its face but it requires giving up the claim that the Gospels preserve faithful chronological reportage. If you grant that the order is editorial, the inerrancy argument as conventionally stated is already conceded.

contradictions.question: How many women came to the sepulchre?
contradictions.summary: John 20:1 says one — Mary Magdalene. Matthew 28:1 says two — Mary Magdalene and 'the other Mary.' Mark 16:1 says three — Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. Luke 24:1, 10 says five or more — Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, 'and other women that were with them.' Each Gospel gives a different number of women at the tomb.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologist response, present in Gleason Archer (Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, Zondervan 1982, pp. 347-349) and pushed harder by John Wenham (Easter Enigma), is the 'one-does-not-exclude-many' move: John mentions Mary Magdalene because she is the focus of his narrative, but he does not deny that others were present. Matthew names two but does not deny the others. Mark names three but does not deny still more. Luke names four and adds 'others.' On this reading, every Gospel is consistent because none of them explicitly denies the presence of additional women. That defense has some logical force, but it strains John 20:2. After finding the tomb empty, Mary Magdalene runs to Peter and the Beloved Disciple and says 'they have taken away the Lord out of the sepulchre, and we know not where they have laid him.' The 'we' is a single anomalous plural in an otherwise solo narrative — and most critical commentators (Brown, Lincoln) read it as a fossil from an earlier multi-woman tradition that John has redacted down to a Mary-only scene for theological reasons. John is editing the tradition, not adding compatible detail. The harmonization also has to deal with the divergent purposes given for the visit: Matthew 28:1 says the women came 'to see the sepulchre,' Mark 16:1 says they came to anoint the body with spices, and John 20:1 has Mary just show up while it is still dark with no stated reason. These differences point to independent and somewhat incompatible traditions about who went, when, and why. The simpler reading: each evangelist had a partial tradition and shaped it for his own narrative. Calling all four texts strictly compatible requires reading 'and others were there too' into each silence.

Matthew 28:2 has the women still on their way when an angel descends from heaven and rolls the stone back in their presence — meaning the tomb was still sealed when they got there.
contradictions.commentary: The Greek of Matthew 28:2 is the problem for harmonizers. The aorist indicative apekulisen ('rolled back') and the angel's act of sitting upon the stone are described as part of the seismos ('earthquake') that occurred at that moment — and Matthew connects this to the women's arrival in the same sentence structure. The most natural reading is that the women witness the angel's descent and the stone's removal. The other three Gospels have the women arrive to find the stone already gone — no angelic descent in their presence, no earthquake. The standard harmonization, articulated by William Lane Craig and earlier by John Wenham, is to read Matthew 28:2 as a flashback — the women didn't witness it, Matthew is just telling the reader how the stone got rolled away at some prior point. The Greek can technically support this if you press kai idou ('and behold') as introducing background information, but the syntax does not naturally cue a flashback the way English narrative would with 'now earlier' or 'meanwhile.' Matthew's narrative flow runs forward: the women set out, an earthquake happens, an angel descends, the guards faint with fear, and the angel speaks to the women. Reading the earthquake-and-descent as having occurred hours earlier requires inserting a temporal break the text does not signal. R. T. France's NICNT commentary on Matthew (Eerdmans 2007, pp. 1098-1100) acknowledges the difficulty and argues for the flashback reading on theological grounds, not grammatical ones. The simpler reading is that Matthew's version has elements (the earthquake, the angelic descent, the fainting guards) that are absent from the other Gospels because Matthew is dramatizing the resurrection event with apocalyptic imagery — and in doing so he has placed events at the tomb that the other evangelists do not include. The flashback move is harmonization by syntactic gymnastics.

contradictions.question: Were the men or angels sitting or standing?
contradictions.summary: Mark 16:5 has the women enter the tomb and find 'a young man sitting on the right side.' John 20:12 has Mary Magdalene see 'two angels in white sitting' — one at the head and one at the feet of where Jesus had lain. Luke 24:3-4 has the women find no body and then 'two men stood by them in shining garments' — actively standing, not sitting.
contradictions.commentary: The detail seems trivial but it's tightly diagnostic. Luke uses the verb epestēsan, which means 'stood beside' or 'stood over' — it describes an active appearance, not a seated reception. Mark has the single figure sitting on the right side of the tomb. John has two angels sitting in fixed positions (head and feet) inside the tomb. Three different choreographies of the same scene. The standard apologetic move, in Wenham and Blomberg, is the sequential reconstruction: the angels were sitting when the women first entered (Mark and John), then stood up at some point during the encounter (Luke). That is a possible if uncreative harmonization. The problem is that Luke's Greek is not 'they stood up' (anestēsan) but 'they stood by' (epestēsan) — and the verb places them already standing when the women see them, not transitioning from a seated position. Luke also has two figures, where Mark has one. The number difference is the bigger contradiction here than the posture. Mark's single-young-man tradition, Matthew's single-angel tradition, Luke's two-men tradition, and John's two-angels tradition cannot all describe the same scene. The standard harmonization that 'one does not exclude two' has the same problem it had in the previous entries: Mark's narrative reads as a complete encounter with one figure, and inserting an invisible second figure is not what the text says. The simpler reading is that each Gospel preserves an independent tradition about the empty-tomb encounter, with different numbers, postures, and locations for the heavenly messenger or messengers. The contradiction is mild taken individually but devastating cumulatively: every detail of the empty-tomb scene differs across the four Gospels, which is exactly what you would expect from independent oral traditions and not from a single eyewitness report.

contradictions.question: Were the men or angels inside or outside the tomb when the when the women arrived?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:2 places the angel outside the tomb, having descended from heaven, rolled the stone back, and seated himself upon it. Mark 16:5 has the women enter the tomb and find a young man sitting inside on the right side. Luke 24:3-4 has the women enter, find no body, and then encounter two men standing 'by them' inside. John 20:11-12 has Mary look into the tomb and see two angels sitting inside. Three Gospels put the messenger(s) inside; Matthew puts him outside, on top of the stone.
contradictions.commentary: Note the question text has a typo — 'when the when the women' — that should be cleaned up by DB maintainers. The contradiction itself is real and clean. Matthew is alone in placing the angel outside, perched on the stone he has just rolled away. The other three Gospels are in agreement that the encounter happens inside the sepulchre. The standard apologetic move is the same composite-narrative reconstruction used throughout the resurrection harmonizations: the women first encountered the outside angel (Matthew), then went inside and encountered another angel or angels (Mark, Luke, John). On this reading, Matthew has telescoped the inside encounter and the other Gospels have telescoped the outside encounter, but all are compatible if you assume two distinct angelic encounters. Wenham develops this at length. The problem is that Matthew's outside angel speaks the same message that Mark's inside young man speaks ('he is not here, for he is risen' — Matthew 28:6, Mark 16:6), and the women are then dismissed with the same instruction to tell the disciples to go to Galilee (Matthew 28:7, Mark 16:7). This is the same speech given by the same character. Matthew has placed it outside the tomb on the stone; Mark has placed it inside. They are not two encounters; they are one encounter located differently. The simpler reading is that Matthew is dramatizing the scene with the descent-and-stone-rolling that the others omit, and in doing so he has relocated the messenger. The composite-encounter reconstruction is a textbook example of harmonization through invention — the second angelic encounter Wenham needs is not in any of the texts. He has to add it to make the puzzle work.

contradictions.question: Did the eleven disciples believe the two men who claimed to see Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Luke 24:33-34 has the two Emmaus disciples return to Jerusalem and find the eleven already saying 'The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Simon' — meaning the eleven already believed, before the Emmaus pair even told their story. Mark 16:12-13 has Jesus appear to two disciples on the road, they report it to the rest, 'neither believed they them.' Same episode, opposite reception.
contradictions.commentary: Mark 16:12-13 is part of the longer ending of Mark, which is missing from the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and is universally treated by textual critics as a second-century addition. So the contradiction is partly a contradiction between a late summarizing addition to Mark and the earlier Lukan tradition. That said, the longer ending of Mark appears to be summarizing Luke's Emmaus story (Luke 24:13-35) — and it gets the reception of the report exactly backwards. Luke is explicit that when the two return, the eleven are already proclaiming the resurrection on the basis of an appearance to Simon. The Markan-ending author seems either to be following a different tradition or simply summarizing carelessly. The standard apologetic move, where this contradiction is addressed at all, is to read Luke and the Markan-ending as describing different reception stages — initial disbelief followed by belief after the Simon appearance. The texts do not support this. Luke 24:33-34 has the eleven proclaiming belief at the moment the Emmaus pair walks in. The Markan-ending has the eleven not believing the Emmaus pair's report. Bruce Metzger and the editors of the United Bible Societies Greek New Testament treat Mark 16:9-20 as a clear later expansion, and its disagreements with Luke are part of the evidence that it is not from the same hand or tradition as the rest of Mark. The cleanest reading is to acknowledge the longer ending of Mark for what it is — a later attempt to give Mark a fuller resurrection ending — and to note that it does not always succeed at staying consistent with the earlier Gospel material it is drawing on.
